entry.title: What observability rollout teaches us about production debugging
entry.summary:
The moment after an alert
Imagine a customer reports a request that failed once and cannot be reproduced locally. A gradual rollout makes it easier to catch overhead, noise, or configuration errors before every service depends on the dashboard. Without a useful record, the team is left comparing assumptions. Start with one low-risk Node.js service and validate data quality, storage, access, and operational usefulness. Begin with the route and time window, correlate nearby application messages, and compare status and duration. Keep a clear distinction between facts in the record and hypotheses about the cause. Capture a baseline, add the instrumentation, compare response behavior, and collect feedback from the people who will use it. Build the smallest safe reproduction from sanitized inputs, add a regression check, and verify the behavior after the change. Set a rollback path and do not treat dashboard availability as a substitute for application health checks. Close the incident by noting what evidence was missing and whether the telemetry policy should change. The useful outcome is a repeatable debugging path, not a bigger pile of logs. Learn more: TracerNest · tracernest-logger on npm

entry.title: I built a photo and video metadata cleaner that runs in the browser and never re-encodes
entry.summary: I made ScrubPic (https://scrubpic.com), a free web tool that shows what is hidden inside a photo or video and saves a clean copy. Here is what it does and a few decisions behind it. The problem. A phone photo can hold GPS coordinates, the phone model, timestamps and the editing apps used. Newer files can also hold Content Credentials (C2PA) and an IPTC "made with AI" tag, which Instagram, Facebook and TikTok read on upload. Most people never see any of it. No upload. The whole job happens in the browser tab. A privacy tool that asks you to upload the private file first felt wrong, so files never leave the device. You can check this: open DevTools › Network while cleaning a file. No re-encoding. Many cleaners redraw the image on a canvas and export it again, which strips the data but also re-compresses the picture. ScrubPic instead removes the metadata blocks from JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC and AVIF files. For MP4, MOV and M4V it turns the metadata boxes into empty free boxes of the same size, so nothing else in the file has to move and the video and audio data stay bit-for-bit the same. Readable output. Instead of a raw tag dump, it lists findings in plain words (location, device, dates, AI records), and you can untick single lines to keep them, e.g. keep the date but drop the location. Limits, stated up front. Invisible watermarks such as SynthID live in the pixels, so no metadata tool removes them. GIF, RAW and MKV aren't supported yet. Removing an AI record from a file doesn't change platform rules on labelling AI content. It's free with no account, meant to be paid for by ads, and the code isn't open source. Feedback welcome, especially files it handles wrongly.
